extracted.intended_audience: psychologists, psychoanalysts, scholars and students of humor/wit
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical-psychological criteria and techniques that generate, shape, and secure the pleasurable effect of witticisms (origination, motives, audience conditions, and technical devices). Derived from Freud's psychoanalytic account of wit and its relation to unconscious processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective determination (personal motives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Witticisms often arise from subjective emotional determinations in the originator (e.g., resentment, self-deprecation), as in Heine's 'famillionaire' born of family mistreatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud cites biographical examples (Heine, neglected cousin; Lichtenberg, hypochondriac eccentricities) to show how personal grievances and emotional history can motivate witty sayings; such subjective roots are persuasive but not claimed to be universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neurotic/psychoneurotic predisposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who originate many witticisms are sometimes found to show dissociated personalities or a predisposition to nervous affections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physicians studying witty individuals have noted neurotic traits, but Freud cautions insufficient data to make this a necessary condition for wit-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-participation as disguised aggression or criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Some witticisms (e.g., certain Jewish witticisms) are made by members of a group about themselves, apparently because they cannot express criticism or aggression directly and thus resort to by-ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when direct expression is difficult—self-directed jokes permit hostile/critical content to be delivered indirectly; example: Heine's joke and Jewish self-deprecating wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambitious impulse / exhibitionism (motive for harmless wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The motive for harmless wit is usually the ambitious impulse to display one's spirit or to 'show off.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud compares this to sexual exhibition; the desire to exhibit can be a primary motive for producing witty remarks intended to impress an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual components and tendency-wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Components of the sexual constitution (e.g., obscene material, sadistic elements) can appear as motives for tendency-wit: obscene jokes conceal a desire to exhibit; strong sadistic sexuality aids aggressive tendency-wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When wit serves sexual or hostile tendencies, it functions as a psychic process among three persons and draws on inhibited impulses turned into wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impulse to impart (wit's social imperative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit-making is inseparably connected with the desire to impart it; wit must usually be communicated to another person to complete the wit-process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike the comic (which can be enjoyed alone), wit requires transmission—originators are compelled to share jokes even overcoming objections to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of the third person (audience) to complete wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit demands another person (the third person) to whom the wit can be imparted; the decision whether a jest has succeeded is transferred to that other person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The third person functions analogously to the 'other' in comic processes; without an appropriate hearer the wit-process is incomplete and the originator may be unable to laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third person's state of mind and social context
rubrics_metrics.description: The third person must be in a jovial or at least indifferent state and devoid of strong opposing feelings; social setting and allegiances (e.g., presence of friends or enemies) determine whether a hearer will laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: no one in an assemblage of divines would laugh at Heine's priest comparison; readiness to laugh requires absence of antagonistic factors and psychic indifference to impediments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychic harmony between originator and audience (shared inhibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third person must be in psychic harmony with the first person and be able to habitually produce the same inner inhibitions that the wit overcame in the originator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared tastes, restraints, and modes of inhibition are necessary—'every witticism thus demands its own public'; lack of shared inhibitions prevents the required discharge and laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy-of-expenditure explanation for hearer's pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The hearer experiences pleasure because he avoids the psychic expenditure that the originator had to make; the wit presents the idea which would otherwise have required effort, so the hearer 'buys the pleasure with little expenditure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud links this economy to the liberation/discharge of inhibition energy in the hearer; the pleasure corresponds to the psychic energy economized or discharged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge mechanism and 'laughter as discharge'
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearer's laughter manifests the release and discharge of psychic inhibition energy that was rendered superfluous when a forbidden idea arose in perception; laughter is a discharge of previously employed psychic energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud references Spencer, Lipps, Bain: laughter as release/detente; in wit the liberated inhibition energy discharges as laughter in the third person rather than (often) in the originator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why the originator often cannot laugh
rubrics_metrics.description: The originator may not laugh because (a) the possibility of discharge is disturbed (energy attached to endopsychic uses), or (b) the originator expends psychic work to produce the wit so that little expendable energy remains for discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the originator experiences wit-pleasure from removing inhibitions, the concurrent psychic work and endopsychic attachments can prevent motor discharge (laughter). Implication: originators must impart wit to procure external discharge/echo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three conditions for liberation/discharge in the third person
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) It must be established that the third person actually produces the expenditure of energy; 2) Care must be taken that when the energy becomes freed it should not find another psychic use instead of motor discharge; 3) It is advantageous only if the energy to be liberated is strengthened and heightened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conditions motivate technical features of wit intended to secure the hearer's automatic discharge rather than diversion of the liberated energy into other mental work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary techniques to secure automatic discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary techniques (omissions, brevity, allusions, facades, comic fore-pleasures) serve to keep conscious attention away so that the wit-process can proceed automatically and permit discharge in the hearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud groups these as techniques that (a) avoid mental effort, (b) divert attention, or (c) provide fore-pleasure, all intended to ensure the hearer discharges rather than re-routes the liberated energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and short expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit strives for the shortest possible expression to expose fewer points of attack to conscious attention and thereby avoid interfering mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity here is tactical—not witty per se—but serves to prevent attention from interrupting the automatic wit-process; overly elaborate wording endangers the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity / easy comprehensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Witticisms must be easily understood; any requirement of mental effort or choice between paths imperils the effect by awakening attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the hearer must perform mental work to get the joke (as in riddles), the laughter effect diminishes or disappears because attention interrupts automatic discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omissions, gaps, and solicitation of completions
rubrics_metrics.description: Omissions in wording and allusive gaps compel the hearer to fill in missing elements, occupying attention just enough to keep the wit-process free from analytic scrutiny and permit discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omissions operate by engaging associative completion without invoking critical mental labor; they help keep the process automatic and facilitate immediate laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogistic facades and representation/contrast devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogistic facades, comic facades, displacement, representation through absurdity, and contrast-of-ideas are technical devices that rivet attention in ways that support, rather than destroy, the automatic wit-process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices either fascinate attention (diverting analytical inspection) or provide comic fore-pleasure that complements wit; Freud warns that some authors over-emphasize 'contrast of ideas' as essential when it functions as a reinforcement technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement and disguised deviation
rubrics_metrics.description: Displacement (answering a question by deviating to another content) can be used openly (obvious displacement) or disguised so the hearer's attention is riveted trying to detect the displacement; disguised displacement is more effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: actress answering 'age' with place of birth; overt displacements are often too conspicuous and less effective than those that compel mental search and thereby assist automatic discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic facade as auxiliary fore-pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic façade promotes wit by (a) riveting attention (facilitating automatism) and (b) furnishing a fore-pleasure via comic discharge which helps the subsequent wit discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes a witticism relies entirely on comic fore-pleasure rather than other wit-techniques; comic elements can thus be used strategically to enhance wit's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and surprise requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit exerts its full effect only when new and surprising; repetition diminishes effect because memory awakens attention to the prior hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains (a) the short-lived nature of witticisms and (b) the producer's desire to impart wit to those who haven't heard it; repetition reduces surprise and thus discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements favoring the wit-process (nonsense, contrast, confusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsense, contrast, and confusion provoke interest and produce a 'psychic damming' (distribution of energy) that heightens the subsequent discharge; 'contrast of ideas' reinforces wit but is not itself the essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements often increase the energy available for discharge and thus the magnitude of laughter; they are technical aids rather than definitional properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damming (psychic damming) to heighten discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: A process of damming—building up inhibition or suspense—precedes and intensifies the discharge when the forbidden or inhibited idea is suddenly allowed, increasing the laugh effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud cites Lipps: the force of discharge varies with the success of the preceding damming; techniques that foster damming therefore enhance wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience specificity ('every witticism demands its own public')
rubrics_metrics.description: Each witticism presupposes a specific public that shares the requisite inhibitions, tastes, and readiness; mismatch between joke and audience prevents the expected effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural, class, or taste differences (e.g., vulgar vs refined audiences) mean the same witticism will be effective only for compatible publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from riddles and facetious questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Witticisms differ from riddles and facetious questions: riddles require mental labor and guessing (which destroys automatic discharge); facetious questions may use techniques but lack the full wit effect because answers are guessable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a witty answer demands analytic effort to 'get' it, the laughter effect disappears; this marks a practical boundary between wit and other comic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy vs alleviation (local savings vs general relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit's apparent economy (saving a particular psychic expenditure) produces momentary pleasure, but full pleasure requires general alleviation through discharge in the third person; wit aims for alleviation rather than mere thrift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud compares psychic economy to business: small savings matter when overall expenditure is large; true pleasure arises when local savings cannot be reallocated and thus become genuine relief.
